name: Moondust Hearth
subtitle: sun-baked rock that keeps rovers alive overnight

effects.effect: a curved mirror focuses light
the moon's dusty surface holds almost no heat
two metals joined at different temperatures make a voltage

how: A night on the Moon lasts two weeks at about minus 170 degrees, and solar-powered landers usually freeze and never wake up. During the long lunar day a mirror focuses sunlight onto a block of packed moon rock until it is hundreds of degrees hot, and a blanket of loose moon dust, which barely passes heat, keeps it hot. Through the night the rover parks beside it, staying warm and drawing a trickle of power from metal junctions that make a voltage when one end is hot and the other cold.
obstacle: The heat-to-electricity junctions turn only about a twentieth of the heat into power, so each rover needs tonnes of baked rock.
real: NASA 'thermal wadi' studies (Balasubramaniam, Wegeng, about 2009-2010); never flown
why: The Moon's own useless dust becomes the thermos; sunlight, rock and dust replace a nuclear heater.

name: Pocket Magnetosphere
subtitle: a magnetic bubble shielding astronauts from radiation

effects.effect: very cold metals lose all electrical resistance
earth's magnetic field traps charged particles in belts
a current makes a magnet

how: Outside Earth's magnetic field, astronauts on a trip to Mars soak up enough radiation to raise their cancer risk sharply, and lead shielding is far too heavy to launch. Rings of wire chilled until they lose all electrical resistance carry a huge current forever without power, making a strong magnetic field around the crew cabin. Just as Earth's field steers charged particles from the Sun into its outer belts, this field bends the particles away from the cabin.
obstacle: Turning aside the most energetic cosmic rays needs coils weighing many tonnes, and a magnet failure in deep space has no repair crew.
real: ESA SR2S superconducting shield study (2013-2015), design only
why: Copies Earth's own planetary defence at cabin scale, made possible because superconducting coils need no power.

name: Comet Steerer
subtitle: mirrors that boil an asteroid off course

effects.effect: a curved mirror focuses light
latent heat
reaction thrust

how: If an icy asteroid is found heading for Earth, smashing it risks breaking it into many pieces still on course. A swarm of mirror spacecraft fly beside it and focus sunlight onto one spot, boiling its ice and rock into a jet of vapour. Like a slow rocket made of the asteroid itself, that jet pushes it gently aside over months, with no fuel carried from Earth.
obstacle: It needs years of warning, and the vapour it makes keeps fogging the very mirrors that make it.
real: 'Mirror Bees' concept (Vasile, University of Strathclyde, about 2010); NASA's DART hit an asteroid instead (2022)
why: Sunlight plus the target's own ice becomes a rocket engine bolted on by mirrors alone.

name: Rain Field
subtitle: dark solar farms that coax clouds into rain

effects.effect: sun-heated air at the equator drives steady winds
air pressure falls the higher you go
droplets form around a seed

how: Coastal deserts often have moist sea air blowing overhead that never rains. A large field of dark solar panels near the coast soaks up sunlight and heats the air above it, which rises like a hot-air balloon; as it climbs into thinner air it expands and cools until its moisture condenses on dust and sea salt into clouds and showers. The same panels make electricity all day.
obstacle: It needs tens of square kilometres of panels beside a humid sea breeze, and no one has shown the rain falls where it's wanted.
real: Only computer models so far (Li et al., Science 2018; Branch and Wulfmeyer 2019)
why: A power plant whose waste heat is the rain-maker: sun, rising air and dust in sequence.

name: Sunlit Feather
subtitle: sunlight-floated sensors for the edge of space

effects.effect: gas molecules push harder off the warm side
air pressure falls the higher you go

how: Between 50 and 80 kilometres up, the air is too thin for balloons or planes and too thick for satellites, so we barely measure a layer that shapes climate and space weather. A wafer thinner than paper, dark on its underside, is warmed by sunlight; air molecules bounce off the warm side harder than off the cool side, the same push that spins a radiometer's vanes. In air that thin each molecule's kick counts, so the push adds up to enough lift to float the wafer and a tiny sensor.
obstacle: The lift is so slight that a working sensor, radio and antenna must weigh only milligrams.
real: Lab levitation in low-pressure chambers (Azadi et al. 2021; Schafer et al., Nature 2025); none flown
why: The radiometer's toy push only becomes lift where air is thin, which is exactly where nothing else flies.

name: Frostwing
subtitle: an airliner whose cold fuel chills its motors

effects.effect: hydrogen liquefies only far below freezing
some ceramics lose all resistance at liquid-nitrogen cold
a reaction drives a current

how: Flying is one of the hardest things to make carbon-free, because batteries are far too heavy for long trips. This plane carries hydrogen as an ultra-cold liquid; on its way to the fuel cells, which turn it into electricity and water, the fuel first flows past the motors and cables, chilling special ceramics until they carry current with no resistance at all. The motors become several times lighter and lose almost no power to heat.
obstacle: Liquid hydrogen takes about four times the space of jet fuel, and no airport supplies it.
real: Airbus ASCEND superconducting powertrain ground test (2023) and Cryoprop concept; nothing has flown
why: One cold liquid does two jobs: fuel and the refrigerant that makes superconducting motors practical.

name: Jetstream Post
subtitle: balloon freight riding high winds across oceans

effects.effect: fast steady winds blow high in the sky
hydrogen is fourteen times lighter than air
lift

how: Air freight burns huge amounts of fuel, while ships take weeks. A hydrogen balloon lifts a parcel pod up to the jet stream, where steady winds of 200 kilometres an hour carry it across an ocean in two or three days; it rises or sinks to pick the wind layer heading the right way. Near the destination it drops a small glider that flies the parcel down to a runway.
obstacle: The winds choose the route, so steering by height alone can miss the target by hundreds of kilometres, and air-traffic rules don't allow unpiloted freight balloons.
real: Japanese Fu-Go balloons crossed the Pacific on the jet stream (1944-45); Loon steered balloons by altitude (2013-2021)
why: Free wind, free lift and a glider's final steering together make fuel-free intercontinental freight.

name: Tame Tornado
subtitle: a man-made whirlwind that spins power turbines

effects.effect: heating a gas expands it
latent heat

how: Power stations and factories dump enormous amounts of lukewarm water heat into the air. Fed into the bottom of a round walled arena through angled vents, that warm, moist air rises and spins into a tall whirlwind; as it climbs, its water vapour condenses and releases more heat, keeping the column rising kilometres high like a thunderstorm's updraft. Air rushing in at the base to replace it drives turbines around the arena's rim.
obstacle: No one knows yet whether a whirlwind tall enough to pay can be kept steady and safely in its arena.
real: Louis Michaud's atmospheric vortex engine; small prototypes in Ontario (about 2012-2016)
why: Waste heat lights the whirlwind, then condensing vapour feeds it; a free chimney kilometres tall.

name: Thawing Road
subtitle: road patches that heat only where ice forms

effects.effect: a magnet loses its magnetism when hot enough
induction

how: Icy roads cause thousands of crashes every winter, and salting them poisons rivers. Coils under the road make a rapidly flipping magnetic field that heats grains of a special magnetic alloy mixed into the asphalt. That alloy stops being magnetic just above freezing, so warm patches switch themselves off and only the icy spots keep drawing power.
obstacle: Alloys that lose their magnetism near freezing, like gadolinium mixes, are expensive, and a road needs tonnes of them plus coils under every lane.
real: Curie-point self-limiting heaters (Metcal soldering irons, 1980s); induction-heated self-healing asphalt (Delft, 2010s)
why: Each grain is its own thermostat, so the road spends energy only on ice.

name: Ember Lantern
subtitle: a cookstove whose glow charges lights and phones

effects.effect: hot things glow
each metal colours a flame its own colour
photoelectric effect

how: Hundreds of millions of people cook on fires every evening but have no electricity for lights or phones. A gas-lamp-style mantle made of ytterbium oxide sits in the flame and glows mostly in one near-infrared colour, the colour ordinary silicon solar cells turn into current best. Cells wrapped around the flame turn that glow into electricity while dinner cooks.
obstacle: Keeping the cells cool and clean beside a smoky wood fire, at a price villagers can afford.
real: Ytterbia-emitter thermophotovoltaics (1990s); JX Crystals 'Midnight Sun' gas stove (about 2000)
why: Flame colour matched to cell colour: the gas-mantle trick of 1885 tuned for solar cells.

name: Lukewarm Battery
subtitle: turns factory warm water into electricity

effects.effect: adding more of one chemical pushes a reaction forward
a reaction drives a current

how: Most waste heat from factories and power plants is lukewarm water, below 80 degrees, too cool for turbines, so it is simply thrown away. This copper battery runs when ammonia is added to one side, because the ammonia grabs copper and pulls the reaction forward. When it runs down, the lukewarm water gently boils the ammonia off and over to the other side, swapping the battery's ends so it runs again.
obstacle: Power per litre is still low, and copper slowly drifts through the membrane, wearing the cell out.
real: Thermally regenerative ammonia battery, lab scale (Penn State, 2014)
why: A still recharges a battery: heat too weak for engines moves a chemical that drives current.

name: Carbon Snowfall
subtitle: freezing carbon dioxide out of Antarctic air

effects.effect: cold plus pressure turns gases into liquids
an expanding gas cools itself

how: To halt climate change we must pull carbon dioxide back out of the air, and most methods need lots of heat or chemicals. Antarctic winter air is already near minus 80 degrees; a plant there squeezes it and lets it expand through a valve, cooling it further until the carbon dioxide frosts out as dry-ice snow while the rest of the air passes through. The carbon snow is stored in insulated pits in the ice.
obstacle: Carbon dioxide only frosts out of air near minus 140 degrees, so the last chilling costs a lot of energy, from wind farms that must be built on the ice sheet.
why: Uses the coldest place on Earth as a free head start on liquefying air.

name: Spark Matchmaker
subtitle: electric fields that snap drug molecules together

effects.effect: lopsided molecules twist to line up in an electric field
two molecules snap together into a ring

how: Making medicines and plastics takes heat, solvents and costly metal catalysts that end up as waste. Here the chemicals flow between closely spaced charged plates; the strong electric field twists lopsided molecules so their reactive ends face each other, and they snap together into rings far faster. Flip the field off and the reaction stops, with nothing to filter out afterwards.
obstacle: The effect has only been shown for single molecules in a tiny gap; scaling the needed field to a whole reactor is unsolved.
real: Electric field sped one Diels-Alder reaction in a microscope junction (Aragonès et al., Nature 2016)
why: A switch replaces a catalyst: alignment by field makes the snap-together reaction happen on demand.

name: Skyward Fridge
subtitle: a vaccine fridge that dumps heat into space

effects.effect: heat radiates as invisible light
latent heat

how: Many vaccines spoil in clinics without reliable electricity because the fridge fails. A mirror-like panel on the roof reflects sunlight but glows away heat as invisible infrared light at a colour the air lets straight through to cold outer space, so it stays below air temperature even at noon. It chills water into a bank of ice around an insulated vaccine box, and the ice melting slowly holds the box cold through cloudy days.
obstacle: Humid tropical air blocks much of the infrared escape route, cutting the cooling just where it's needed most.
real: Daytime radiative-cooling panels (Stanford, 2014; SkyCool Systems for buildings, about 2019); not yet as an off-grid vaccine fridge
why: Outer space is the heat sink: a sky-facing panel plus ice replaces compressor and power.
